      Important plan information

      About the technology

      An FTTN or FTTB connection uses the existing copper network from a nearby street cabinet in your neighbourhood or from your building’s communications room.

      An FTTC connection uses the existing copper network from a nearby pit on your street.

      An FTTP connection uses a optical-fibre cable from a nearby fibre node.

      Getting connected

      If your home is connected using FTTN or FTTB, you’ll need a Wi-Fi router with a built-in VDSL2 modem compatible with the nbn® network. You can order one of these when applying for a service.

      If your home is connected using FTTC or FTTP, you’ll need a Wi-Fi router to share your connection your computers and wireless devices. You can order one of these when applying for a service.

      nbn® co’s New Developments Charge

      In line with the Australian Government’s Telecommunications Infrastructure in New Developments Policy, nbn® co implemented the New Developments Charge on 2 April 2016. A premises identified by nbn® co as a New Development Location is subject to nbn® co’s once-off New Developments Charge if the premises has never had an active nbn™ service. Despite its name, the New Developments Charge also applies to New Development Locations that were built years ago. It even applies to premises where nbn® co has already installed the equipment necessary to connect the premises to the nbn™ network.

      The New Developments Charge does not apply if there has been already been an active nbn™ service connected at the premises, and it doesn’t apply if the premises hasn’t been identified by nbn® co as a New Development Location.

      Best nbn® Plan

      If you are looking for the best nbn® plan available, you may have tried searching online to find good deals. But there are so many plans to choose from – not to mention the different connection types, data caps, and logistics to consider – that it can be hard to determine which one is best for your needs.

      While urban areas can more easily access high-speed internet services, regional areas may find it difficult to access anything reliable.

      If you are looking for the best nbn® plan that offers fast internet speeds at an affordable price, then Skymesh may have the solution for you. We specialise in helping regional Australians connect to fast and reliable internet. We offer a range of nbn® plans that are suitable for both households and businesses.

      Read more

      How fast are nbn® internet plans?

      Those in search of the best nbn® plan will find that the network already has each address assigned to the type of connection that’s best for them based on the area’s location, infrastructure, and population density. The speed of nbn® internet plans can vary depending on a number of factors, including the type of nbn® technology used in your area, the plan you choose, and the capacity of the nbn® network in your location.

      Skymesh offers three speed tiers for plans using Fixed Line technologies.

      The nbn® 25 tier is ideal for small groups of two people and provides ideal speeds for activities like sending emails, surfing the web, and video streaming. This service plan has typical evening speeds of up to 25 Mbps download and up to 4 Mbps upload between 7.00 p.m. and 11.00 p.m.

      The nbn® 50 tier is good for up to three people and offers speeds that are able to manage web browsing, social media, online gaming, and more. This tier has typical evening speeds of up to 48 Mbps download and up to 17 Mbps upload between 7.00 p.m. and 11.00 p.m.

      Lastly, the nbn® 100 tier is suitable for groups of more than four people and supplies very fast speeds that can accommodate more demanding tasks such as ultra high-definition streaming and gaming, downloading large files, and telecommuting. Users can enjoy typical evening speeds of up to 98 Mbps download and up to 17 Mbps upload between 7.00 p.m. and 11.00 p.m.

      Is nbn® better than a wireless broadband connection?

      You might be wondering how nbn® compares to home wireless broadband, a type of connection that connects you to the internet remotely using 4G or 5G networks.

      If you are comparing 5G vs nbn®, 4G and 5G home wireless connections could be a viable option for improving your internet experience, depending on their availability in your location. However, the speed of these connections may not be as reliable because they are more prone to congestion.

      nbn® is generally better than a home wireless broadband connection for regional Australia. The network uses fibre, satellite, and other technologies to deliver the best nbn® plan and connection type for each area. This means that it can provide broadband services to even the most remote areas that are not covered by traditional networks.

      The best nbn® setup for you would depend on your location. nbn® also offers wireless broadband services through nbn® Fixed Wireless, which uses radio signals and outdoor antennas to connect your premises to an nbn® network. Customers may also be able to connect through Sky Muster™ technology, which uses cutting-edge satellites in space and a satellite internet dish installed on your roof to give you connectivity, even in truly off-the-grid locations.

      Apart from Fixed Wireless and satellite options, nbn® also uses Fixed Line technology. It uses fibre optic cables, making it faster than traditional connections, depending on distance and copper quality.

      There are different types of technologies involved, including Fibre to the Premises (FTTP), Fibre to the Building (FTTB), Fibre to the Node (FTTN), Fibre to the Curb (FTTC), and Hybrid Fibre Coaxial (HFC). Some Fixed Line connections may utilise the existing copper network as the last part of an nbn® connection or use hybrid connections, which can affect the speed of the service, depending on the age and capabilities of the copper network going into the premises.

      How much does nbn® cost month to month?

      The cost of an nbn® connection will vary depending on a few factors, such as the type of connection, the service speed, and the plan chosen.

      The average household in Australia pays around $73 per month for their nbn® service. You also have multiple speed tiers to choose from, and the plan you choose can affect the price.
      Eligible customers may be able to enjoy free standard installations for their nbn® internet plans.* However, nbn®-imposed charges may apply in certain instances.

      Looking at the average prices can help you get a rough estimate of the best nbn® plan for your budget. However, instead of immediately looking for the cheapest WiFi option, it might be better to prioritise the speed tier suitable for your daily usage and then set your budget accordingly.

      For those in search of BYO modem nbn® plans, we only offer limited support for nbn®-compatible routers. You must be comfortable configuring them yourself. For your convenience, you can purchase a Skymesh plug-n-play router with free shipping and standard tech support.

      If you are having difficulty understanding all the different plans and options available to you, we invite you to call us at 1300 759 637.

      We have friendly and knowledgeable customer service representatives that are happy to assist you and help you find the best nbn® plan for your needs. You can ask anything about fibre to home, fibre to node, HFC, or other connection types that may be available at your location.

      Even though some internet service providers outsource their customer service to overseas call centres, we believe local knowledge and skills are necessary to comprehend the unique connectivity challenges of Australians. That’s why our customer care staff is made up of Brisbane-based regional internet professionals who understand the local internet scene and can help you out with your questions.

        Actual speeds

        Data speeds for the Service are variable and are suitable for basic Internet connectivity. The actual speed you will experience at any given time will vary depending on various factors including network (signal, proximity, line of sight or congestion), location (modem placement, distance from the wireless tower, geography, obstructions), weather, hardware and software.

        Your speed will typically be less than the limits imposed by the wholesale network. When we have enough reliable data, we will publish typical busy-period speeds.

        Speeds may differ from third-party mobile access services on the same network.
